title: Workflow
text:
The Climate Knowledge Graph (CKG) workflow turns an unstructured climate science corpus into structured, queryable, and publishable knowledge. Beginning with IPCC AR6 sources, the process moves through harvesting, knowledge modelling, Wikibase import, annotation, analysis, and publication outputs. The result is a FAIR, linked data environment that supports both research and publication-ready outputs.


flowchart LR
    A[Identify AR6 sources<br/>authors, glossary, references] --> B[Harvest corpus<br/>web and PDF content]
    B --> C[Create initial data model]
    C --> D[Import structured data into Wikibase]
    D --> E[Map report navigation<br/>MediaWiki categories and links]
    E --> F[Enrich entities<br/>authors, glossary, acronyms, bibliographic data]
    F --> G[Annotate and validate<br/>community review and linking]
    G --> H[Analyse and visualise<br/>Wikibase data and graphs]
    G --> I[Publish outputs<br/>API, HTML, PDF, notebooks, LLM interfaces]
    H --> J[FAIR linked open data]
    I --> K[Shareable publications and services]



Working with the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report (AR6) corpus, the project follows a sequence of stages that convert source material into structured knowledge and reusable publication outputs.

Identify relevant report sources and metadata, including authors, glossary terms, acronyms, references, and bibliographic material.
Harvest the report corpus from web and PDF sources.
Design an initial knowledge graph data model suited to the report structure and research use cases.
Import the data into Wikibase as the central knowledge graph store.
Link the report content to media and navigation structures in MediaWiki for browsing and discovery.
Harvest and import additional supporting data such as authors, glossary terms, acronyms, references, and bibliographic records.
Annotate the report using the imported data and related entities.
Support community annotation and review through established knowledge-sharing communities and linked-data workflows.
Map relevant data to Wikidata and related knowledge structures where appropriate.
Perform analysis, visualisation, and data exploration over the resulting graph.
Generate publication outputs from the graph using computational publishing workflows.
Deliver searchable, shareable, and machine-readable outputs such as REST APIs, RDF data, HTML publications, and LLM-ready knowledge services.

Purpose
Outputs

Authors, glossary, acronyms, references, bibliographic fields

Structured text and document corpus

Initial ER/data model


Wikibase import
Load core entities and metadata into the knowledge graph
Structured graph data


Navigation and linking
Connect report content to browsable structures
MediaWiki categories, report links, entity navigation


Enrichment
Add supporting data and metadata
Glossary, author records, bibliographic details, references


Annotation and review
Add semantic meaning and community validation
Linked report content, collaborative annotations


Analysis and visualisation
Query and explore knowledge graph data
Graph analysis, summaries, figures, derived insights


Publication
Turn graph content into shareable outputs
REST API, HTML, notebooks, PDF-like layouts, machine-readable data


FAIR data services
Make knowledge reusable and interoperable
RDF export, API access, linked open data, publication services






The publication layer uses a computational publishing service that turns Wikibase content into HTML and other formats. This approach supports multi-format publishing, including PDF-like layouts via paged media CSS, while keeping the underlying knowledge in the graph so it can be reused for search, analysis, and machine-readable outputs.

title: Project Roadmap
text:
Climate Knowledge Graph (ClimateKG)
Status: In progress


ClimateKG aims to turn the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report into a reusable, navigable, and FAIR knowledge graph. The project brings together report structure, bibliographic metadata, glossary terms, citations, and data into a semantic layer that supports search, analysis, and publication workflows for policy, research, and public engagement.



The roadmap follows the priorities set out in issue #236 and the project report, with the following milestones:

Lock down the ER model
Add common schemas
Add missing IPCC glossary terms
Release the question bank
Add citations
Add data
Add WG1 figures to the data from GitHub
Add front matter and back matter







Finalise the entity-relationship model for the document corpus.
Consolidate common schemas for report structure, bibliographic metadata, author data, glossary entries, and references.
Stabilise the knowledge graph data model so the project can support community contributions without breaking the underlying structure.





Add the missing glossary terms and resolve gaps in terminology coverage.
Add citations and cross-reference data needed for reliable discovery and provenance.
Capture figure, dataset, and chapter-level metadata in a consistent model.
Extend coverage into front matter and back matter to complete the document structure.





Add the remaining data sources required for the report corpus, including structured data and supporting metadata.
Add WG1 figures and related data from the GitHub-based source material.
Integrate the question bank as a reusable access layer for research and community engagement.
Prepare publication outputs for multiple channels, including HTML, structured data, and reusable query-based access.





Support analysis workflows for data scientists and citizen science contributors.
Link project data to open scholarly infrastructures and metadata services.
Develop a clear review and contribution process for adding data to the knowledge graph.
Maintain compatibility with the publishing and data distribution objectives of the project.








AR6 source material has been harvested and normalised.
Supporting metadata sources have been identified and structured.
The knowledge graph model has been prototyped and reviewed.
Publishing and distribution pathways have been explored with Wikibase and associated tooling.
The project has demonstrated document distribution and data-access workflows.





Finalise the ER model and schema layer.
Complete missing glossary and citation data.
Add the remaining corpus data and WG1 figure assets.
Replace provisional structures with a stable public-facing deployment path.
Expand publication and analysis tooling for community use.





The project builds from the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report and the surrounding metadata ecosystem to create a sample of a future climate knowledge infrastructure: structured, linked, and reusable. The roadmap therefore focuses on establishing a robust foundation for the report corpus first, then expanding community analysis, publication, and semantic distribution services on top of that foundation.




AR6: IPCC Sixth Assessment Report
ER model: entity-relationship model for the document corpus
FAIR: findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable
Wikibase: structured data platform used for the knowledge graph
#semanticClimate: project partner and open research community contributing to the climate knowledge effort

title: About
text:
Climate Knowledge Graph (ClimateKG) is a community knowledge graph for literature on climate change science, intended for use by policymakers, citizen science projects, and scientists.
ClimateKG is a software research project for constructing a knowledge graph using the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s Sixth Assessment Report with the Wikibase software platform. The FAIR Principles are being applied to publishing and are employed to enrich the report with granular cataloguing, document distribution, and data analysis. The knowledge graph is a ‘community knowledge graph’ targeted at policymakers, citizen science projects, and scientists — inviting contributions and engagement to increase the report’s impact.
As a starting point, ClimateKG has imported the main sections of the 10,000 page corpus IPCC Sixth Assessment Report into the knowledge graph.
On the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report:

It is a survival guide for humanity. As it shows, the 1.5-degree limit is achievable.  - UN Secretary-General António Guterres (2023)




ClimateKG: Browse the text and data
ClimateKG Data Bench: Data analysis and community contributions
Docs: Documentation and development log








The objective is to add a data surface to what is already in the documents, making the knowledge usable and searchable.
ClimateKG converts the Sixth Assessment Report from the web into basic foundational datasets to capture their main parts. It then connects these components using an entity-relationship model. The result is a knowledge graph: structured and connected data that can be searched directly.


AR6 has been broken down into five foundational datasets:







Dataset
Data




1. Corpus full text & structure
7 reports; 88 chapters; 7,524,958 words, and; 2,153 image files


2. Bibliographic information
95 DOIs


3. Glossary terms
1,274 terms


4. Acronyms
1,910


5. Authors
932






ClimateKG connects these datasets using an entity-relationship model, forming the knowledge graph:
+- Corpus structure
+- 7 reports
   +- REPORT
   |  <- Bibliographic information
   |  <- Glossary terms
   |  <- Acronyms
   +- CHAPTER
         <- Authors
         <- Bibliographic information
         <- Corpus full text




ClimateKG is a community knowledge graph that supports contributions from the scientific community and engagement from the wider public.


The connections that the knowledge graph creates allow for querying the data. For example, given the question:

‘How many South American or Indian authors contributed to the report?’

ClimateKG can retrieve the answer along with the relevant chapter texts:

‘AR6 author distribution is 71 from South America and 43 from India.’















Document distribution: The data provides a map of the internal structure of the corpus documents, enabling any section or piece of data to be retrieved and delivered to the user.
Extended metadata: Questions can be answered quickly and reliably. Metadata is distributed to library systems and the Data Commons on Wikidata.
Citizen science: ClimateKG collaborates with Youth Data Champions interns from the #SemanticClimate organisation on a global scale.
Data science community: Contributors can enrich the corpus while maintaining the integrity of the original documents.





Inspired by Tim Berners-Lee’s vision of the Semantic Web, ClimateKG is a software R&D project that uses FAIR Principles and Open Science infrastructures to liberate literature on climate change science.


ClimateKG has been funded by TIB Innovation fund, TIB — Leibniz Information Centre for Science and Technology and University Library of Hannover (ROR ID: ror.org/04aj4c181)
ClimateKG is an R&D project hosted at TIB — Leibniz Information Centre for Science and Technology and University Library — Germany, in partnership with #semanticClimate and the National Institute of Plant Genome Research (NIPGR) — India.



ClimateKG comes out of the #semanticClimate (#sC) open research group founded by Dr. Gitanjali Yadav of NIPGR, Delhi, Dr Peter Murray-Rust of Cambridge University, and Simon Worthington (TIB). #semanticClimate supports an India-wide internship programme, hackathon series, and youth outreach programme. Web: https://semanticclimate.github.io/
TIB is one of the largest science libraries in the world and a global hub for knowledge graph R&D, especially the Open Research Knowledge Graph (ORKG). ClimateKG partners with Lab Knowledge Infrastructures led by Dr Markus Stocker, and draws on expertise from NFDI4Culture projects: Wikibase4Research, Computational Publishing Service, and Antelope (terminology service).



Project lead, Simon Worthington — #bookliberationist and publishing technologist simon.worthington@tib.eu ORCID iD: 0000-0002-8579-9717 | Mastodon: @mrchristian
Laura Oldenbourg — data modeling and publishing specialist, ORCID iD: 0009-0003-5070-0099.
With support from Markus Stocker, lead of Lab Knowledge Infrastructures.
Thank you for support and contributions to TIB colleagues and #semanticClimate members, volunteers, interns, and hackathon participants.

title: About us
text:
About us
Climate Knowledge Graph (ClimateKG) is a community knowledge graph for literature on climate change science, intended for use by policymakers, citizen science projects, and scientists.
ClimateKG is a software research project for constructing a knowledge graph using the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s Sixth Assessment Report with the Wikibase software platform. The FAIR Principles are being applied to publishing and are employed to enrich the report with granular cataloguing, document distribution, and data analysis. The knowledge graph is a ‘community knowledge graph’ targeted at policymakers, citizen science projects, and scientists — inviting contributions and engagement to increase the report’s impact.
As a starting point, ClimateKG has imported the main sections of the 10,000 page corpus IPCC Sixth Assessment Report into the knowledge graph.
